points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 3: Design process: defining problems and developing ideas
points.title: Discover
points.detail: Researching the problem, the client, the audience and the context, and gathering inspiration before generating solutions.

questions.q: Explain what happens during the discover phase and why designers resist generating solutions immediately.
answer: The designer researches the problem, the client, the intended audience and the context in which the communication will be encountered.
Existing solutions and comparable work are analysed to understand conventions and to identify opportunities.
Generating solutions immediately locks the designer into the first idea, which is usually the most obvious and least distinctive.
Research also reveals constraints and audience expectations that would otherwise force expensive changes later in the process.

card.title: Discover
back: Researching the problem, the client, the audience and the context, and gathering inspiration before generating solutions.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 3: Design process: defining problems and developing ideas
points.title: Define
points.detail: Synthesising research into a clear statement of the problem to be solved, the communication need and the criteria for success.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of the define phase and what a well-framed design problem statement contains.
answer: The define phase converts research findings into a focused statement of the actual problem, which is often different from the one originally presented.
A well-framed statement identifies the audience, the communication need and the context, without prescribing the solution.
Leaving the solution open allows a wider range of ideas to be explored in the next phase.

card.title: Define
back: Synthesising research into a clear statement of the problem to be solved, the communication need and the criteria for success.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 3: Design process: defining problems and developing ideas
points.title: Develop and ideation
points.detail: Divergent generation of many ideas through thumbnails, sketching, brainstorming and mind mapping, then convergent selection and refinement.

questions.q: Explain the difference between divergent and convergent thinking in ideation and why both are needed.
answer: Divergent thinking generates a large quantity of varied ideas without evaluating them, using rapid techniques such as thumbnails and brainstorming.
Convergent thinking then evaluates those ideas against the brief and criteria to select the strongest for development.
Quantity matters in the divergent phase because early ideas tend to be conventional and the more original concepts emerge later.
Evaluating too early suppresses the unusual ideas that produce distinctive solutions.

card.title: Develop and ideation
back: Divergent generation of many ideas through thumbnails, sketching, brainstorming and mind mapping, then convergent selection and refinement.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 3: Design process: defining problems and developing ideas
points.title: Deliver
points.detail: Refining the chosen concept, resolving technical requirements, producing the final presentation and preparing files for production.

questions.q: Explain what distinguishes a refined concept from a developmental one.
answer: A developmental concept explores an idea and may be rough, partial or unresolved in its detail.
A refined concept resolves every element: composition, typography, colour, scale, alignment and technical specification.
It is presented in a form appropriate to its final use, including correct dimensions, bleed, resolution or file format for production.

card.title: Deliver
back: Refining the chosen concept, resolving technical requirements, producing the final presentation and preparing files for production.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 3: Design process: defining problems and developing ideas
points.title: Iteration and the non-linear process
points.detail: Returning to earlier phases as new information emerges, and treating feedback and testing as part of the process rather than a final step.

questions.q: Explain why the design process is described as iterative rather than linear.
answer: Testing a concept often reveals that the problem was framed incorrectly or that an assumption about the audience was wrong.
The designer then returns to an earlier phase, redefines the problem or generates new ideas, rather than proceeding with a flawed solution.
Iteration produces better outcomes because each cycle incorporates what was learned from the previous one.

card.title: Iteration and the non-linear process
back: Returning to earlier phases as new information emerges, and treating feedback and testing as part of the process rather than a final step.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Line and shape
points.detail: The expressive and structural roles of line, and the distinction between geometric and organic shape and the associations each carries.

questions.q: Explain two functions of line in a visual communication and the associations of geometric versus organic shape.
answer: Line directs the viewer's eye through a composition and can divide or connect areas of the design.
Line also carries expressive quality: a thin, even line reads as precise and controlled, while a thick, irregular line reads as energetic or handmade.
Geometric shapes suggest order, technology and precision, while organic shapes suggest nature, comfort and informality.

card.title: Line and shape
back: The expressive and structural roles of line, and the distinction between geometric and organic shape and the associations each carries.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Form, texture and tone
points.detail: Creating the illusion of three dimensions, the tactile and visual qualities of texture, and the use of tone to model form and create depth.

questions.q: Explain how tone is used to create the illusion of three-dimensional form on a flat surface.
answer: Tone describes the lightness or darkness of an area, and is applied according to a consistent light source.
Surfaces facing the light are rendered lighter, those turned away are darker, and cast shadows anchor the object to a surface.
Gradual tonal transitions suggest curved surfaces, while abrupt changes suggest flat planes meeting at an edge.

card.title: Form, texture and tone
back: Creating the illusion of three dimensions, the tactile and visual qualities of texture, and the use of tone to model form and create depth.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Colour
points.detail: Hue, value and saturation, colour schemes, the psychological and cultural associations of colour, and the difference between RGB and CMYK.

questions.q: Explain the difference between RGB and CMYK and why the distinction matters to a designer.
answer: RGB is an additive colour system used by screens, in which red, green and blue light combine to produce colour.
CMYK is a subtractive system used in printing, in which cyan, magenta, yellow and black inks absorb light.
The RGB gamut is wider, so highly saturated screen colours cannot always be reproduced in print and appear duller.
A designer therefore works in the colour mode matching the final output, and checks print proofs rather than relying on screen appearance.

card.title: Colour
back: Hue, value and saturation, colour schemes, the psychological and cultural associations of colour, and the difference between RGB and CMYK.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Figure-ground and contrast
points.detail: The relationship between positive and negative space, and the use of contrast in size, tone, colour, weight and shape to create emphasis.

questions.q: Explain the figure-ground relationship and how it can be manipulated for effect.
answer: Figure-ground describes the perceptual separation of a subject from its background.
Strong contrast in tone, colour or detail makes the figure read clearly and immediately.
Deliberately ambiguous figure-ground, where the negative space forms a second readable shape, creates a memorable dual image often used in logo design.

card.title: Figure-ground and contrast
back: The relationship between positive and negative space, and the use of contrast in size, tone, colour, weight and shape to create emphasis.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Balance and scale
points.detail: Symmetrical, asymmetrical and radial balance, visual weight, and the use of scale and proportion to establish importance.

questions.q: Distinguish between symmetrical and asymmetrical balance and explain the effect of each.
answer: Symmetrical balance places elements of equal visual weight evenly either side of a central axis.
It reads as formal, stable and traditional, which suits contexts such as certificates and institutional communication.
Asymmetrical balance distributes unequal elements so that their visual weights offset one another without mirroring.
It reads as dynamic and contemporary and creates more visual interest, but requires careful judgement to avoid appearing unresolved.

card.title: Balance and scale
back: Symmetrical, asymmetrical and radial balance, visual weight, and the use of scale and proportion to establish importance.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Hierarchy and emphasis
points.detail: Directing the order in which information is read through size, weight, colour, position and space, and establishing a clear focal point.

questions.q: Explain how visual hierarchy is created and why a poster without it fails.
answer: Hierarchy is created by varying size, weight, colour, contrast, position and surrounding space so elements rank in importance.
The most important information is given the greatest visual weight and is usually positioned where the eye enters the composition.
Without hierarchy every element competes equally for attention, so the viewer does not know where to look first.
A poster is typically viewed for a second or two, so an unclear hierarchy means the core message is never received.

card.title: Hierarchy and emphasis
back: Directing the order in which information is read through size, weight, colour, position and space, and establishing a clear focal point.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Pattern, repetition and rhythm
points.detail: Using repeated elements to create unity and visual rhythm, and the use of variation within repetition to prevent monotony.

questions.q: Explain how repetition creates unity across a multi-page publication.
answer: Repeating consistent typefaces, colours, margins, grid structure and graphic devices across pages establishes a recognisable visual system.
The reader learns the system quickly, so navigating each new page requires less effort.
Deliberate variation within that system, such as a differently treated opening page, provides emphasis without breaking the overall unity.

card.title: Pattern, repetition and rhythm
back: Using repeated elements to create unity and visual rhythm, and the use of variation within repetition to prevent monotony.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Proximity, alignment and space
points.detail: Grouping related elements, aligning to an invisible structure, and using white space deliberately rather than treating it as leftover.

questions.q: Explain the principles of proximity and alignment and why white space should be treated as an active element.
answer: Proximity groups related items closely and separates unrelated ones, so the viewer perceives the structure of the information before reading it.
Alignment relates every element to a shared edge or axis, which produces a sense of order even in an asymmetrical layout.
White space is not empty space; it creates the separation that makes proximity legible and gives emphasis to what it surrounds.
Cramming the page to fill it destroys both grouping and emphasis, making the design harder to read rather than more informative.

card.title: Proximity, alignment and space
back: Grouping related elements, aligning to an invisible structure, and using white space deliberately rather than treating it as leftover.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Manual drawing methods
points.detail: Freehand sketching, technical drawing, rendering and the appropriate use of each at different stages of the process.

questions.q: Explain why freehand thumbnail sketching is used early in the process rather than digital rendering.
answer: Thumbnails are fast, so many compositional alternatives can be explored in the time one digital version would take.
Their roughness keeps attention on composition and hierarchy rather than on detail and finish.
Being quick and disposable, they also reduce the reluctance to abandon an idea that is not working.

card.title: Manual drawing methods
back: Freehand sketching, technical drawing, rendering and the appropriate use of each at different stages of the process.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Technical drawing conventions
points.detail: Orthogonal drawing with third angle projection, isometric, planometric and perspective drawing, and the conventions of scale and dimensioning.

questions.q: Distinguish between orthogonal and perspective drawing and state when each is appropriate.
answer: Orthogonal drawing presents separate two-dimensional views of an object, typically front, side and top, drawn to scale with no distortion.
It is used for technical documentation and manufacture because true dimensions can be measured directly from the drawing.
Perspective drawing represents the object as the eye would see it, with parallel lines converging at vanishing points.
It is used for presentation and client communication because it conveys appearance persuasively, but it cannot be measured for production.

card.title: Technical drawing conventions
back: Orthogonal drawing with third angle projection, isometric, planometric and perspective drawing, and the conventions of scale and dimensioning.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Two-point perspective
points.detail: Horizon line, vanishing points and the construction of forms receding to two points, and the effect of eye level on the view.

questions.q: Explain the role of the horizon line and vanishing points in a two-point perspective drawing.
answer: The horizon line represents the viewer's eye level within the scene.
Two vanishing points are placed on the horizon line, and all receding horizontal edges converge to one or the other.
Vertical edges remain vertical and parallel to one another.
Placing the horizon line low makes the object appear imposing, while a high horizon produces a view looking down on it.

card.title: Two-point perspective
back: Horizon line, vanishing points and the construction of forms receding to two points, and the effect of eye level on the view.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Digital methods
points.detail: Vector and raster software, the difference between the two file types, resolution, and the use of layers, masks and type tools.

questions.q: Explain the difference between vector and raster images and when each should be used.
answer: A vector image is defined by mathematical paths, so it can be scaled to any size without loss of quality.
A raster image is a grid of pixels, so enlarging it beyond its native resolution produces visible pixellation.
Vectors suit logos, type and illustration that must reproduce at many sizes, from a business card to a billboard.
Rasters suit photographs and images with continuous tonal variation, and must be supplied at adequate resolution for the intended output size.

card.title: Digital methods
back: Vector and raster software, the difference between the two file types, resolution, and the use of layers, masks and type tools.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Models, mock-ups and prototypes
points.detail: Producing physical and digital models to test form, scale and function, and presenting concepts in context.

questions.q: Explain the value of presenting a design as a mock-up in context rather than as a flat file.
answer: A mock-up shows the design at its actual scale and in the setting where the audience will encounter it.
This reveals problems invisible on screen, such as text too small to read at viewing distance or a logo that fails on a curved surface.
It also communicates the concept to a client more persuasively, since they can judge the effect rather than imagine it.

card.title: Models, mock-ups and prototypes
back: Producing physical and digital models to test form, scale and function, and presenting concepts in context.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Typeface classification
points.detail: Serif, sans serif, script, display and monospaced typefaces, their characteristics and the associations each carries.

questions.q: Distinguish between serif and sans serif typefaces and explain the associations of each.
answer: Serif typefaces have small strokes at the ends of letterforms, while sans serif typefaces do not.
Serifs are associated with tradition, authority and formality, and have historically been used for extended printed body text.
Sans serif typefaces are associated with modernity, clarity and neutrality, and perform well at small sizes on screen.
The choice should follow the communication's purpose and audience rather than personal preference alone.

card.title: Typeface classification
back: Serif, sans serif, script, display and monospaced typefaces, their characteristics and the associations each carries.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Typographic anatomy and measurement
points.detail: Baseline, x-height, ascender, descender, cap height, counter and stem, and the measurement of type size and leading in points.

questions.q: Explain what x-height is and why two typefaces set at the same point size can appear different in size.
answer: X-height is the height of the lowercase letters without ascenders or descenders, measured from the baseline.
Point size measures the overall type body, not the visible letterforms, so typefaces distribute that space differently.
A typeface with a large x-height appears larger and is generally more legible at small sizes, even at an identical point size.

card.title: Typographic anatomy and measurement
back: Baseline, x-height, ascender, descender, cap height, counter and stem, and the measurement of type size and leading in points.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Legibility and readability
points.detail: Line length, leading, tracking, kerning, alignment and contrast, and their effect on the ease of reading extended text.

questions.q: Distinguish between legibility and readability and name three factors that affect readability in body text.
answer: Legibility is how easily individual characters can be distinguished from one another, a property of the typeface itself.
Readability is how easily extended text can be read, a property of how the type has been set.
Line length affects readability, since very long lines make it difficult to find the start of the next line.
Leading and tracking also affect it, as text set too tightly causes lines to blur together and text set too loosely fragments into separate words.

card.title: Legibility and readability
back: Line length, leading, tracking, kerning, alignment and contrast, and their effect on the ease of reading extended text.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Type hierarchy and pairing
points.detail: Establishing levels of information through size, weight, case and colour, and combining typefaces with sufficient contrast.

questions.q: Explain how to establish a three-level type hierarchy and the principle governing typeface pairing.
answer: Differentiate the levels using changes in size, weight, case and colour rather than by changing typeface for each level.
A heading may be large and bold, a subheading smaller and medium weight, and body text smaller again in regular weight.
When pairing typefaces, contrast must be clear, typically by combining a serif with a sans serif.
Two typefaces that are similar but not identical read as an error rather than a deliberate pairing, so either contrast strongly or use one family's weights.

card.title: Type hierarchy and pairing
back: Establishing levels of information through size, weight, case and colour, and combining typefaces with sufficient contrast.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 2: Design analysis
points.title: Images and photography in design
points.detail: Selecting, cropping and treating images, the effect of viewpoint and framing, and the integration of image with type.

questions.q: Explain how cropping changes the meaning of a photograph in a design.
answer: Cropping removes context, so the viewer's attention is directed to what remains rather than to the whole scene.
A tight crop on a face creates intimacy and emotional emphasis, while a wide crop emphasises setting and scale.
Cropping also changes the image's proportions and its visual weight in the composition, affecting the balance of the layout.

card.title: Images and photography in design
back: Selecting, cropping and treating images, the effect of viewpoint and framing, and the integration of image with type.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 1: Professional design practice
points.title: Communication design
points.detail: Branding, publication, packaging, advertising, signage and digital interface design, and the conventions of each.

questions.q: Explain the requirements of an effective logo.
answer: It must be simple enough to be recognised instantly and recalled after brief exposure.
It must be scalable, working at both business card and billboard size, which favours vector construction and limited detail.
It must be legible in a single colour and in reverse, since it will be applied to varied backgrounds and production methods.
It must be appropriate to the organisation and distinctive within its sector, so that it is not confused with competitors.

card.title: Communication design
back: Branding, publication, packaging, advertising, signage and digital interface design, and the conventions of each.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 1: Professional design practice
points.title: Environmental design
points.detail: Architectural, interior, landscape and exhibition design, the representation of three-dimensional space, and the consideration of human movement and scale.

questions.q: Explain three considerations specific to environmental design that do not apply to communication design.
answer: Human scale and movement, since people occupy and move through the design rather than viewing it from a fixed position.
Structural and material constraints, because the design must be physically buildable and safe.
Site context, including orientation, climate, access and the relationship to surrounding buildings and landscape.
Accessibility and regulatory compliance also impose requirements that a printed communication does not face.

card.title: Environmental design
back: Architectural, interior, landscape and exhibition design, the representation of three-dimensional space, and the consideration of human movement and scale.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 1: Professional design practice
points.title: Industrial design
points.detail: Designing objects and products for manufacture and use, considering ergonomics, materials, production processes and the user's experience.

questions.q: Explain the role of ergonomics in industrial design and give an example of an ergonomic consideration.
answer: Ergonomics is the study of how people physically interact with objects, and it ensures a product can be used comfortably, safely and efficiently.
The designer considers the range of body sizes and capabilities in the intended user group rather than a single average user.
An example is sizing and shaping a handle so it can be gripped securely by users with differing hand sizes and grip strength.

card.title: Industrial design
back: Designing objects and products for manufacture and use, considering ergonomics, materials, production processes and the user's experience.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 1: Professional design practice
points.title: Design conventions across fields
points.detail: The different presentation formats, drawing types and audiences appropriate to each design field.

questions.q: Explain why the presentation format for an environmental design proposal differs from that for a brand identity.
answer: An environmental design must communicate three-dimensional space, so it uses plans, elevations, sections and perspective renderings.
A brand identity must communicate consistent application, so it uses the logo at various sizes, colour variants and mock-ups across media.
The presentation format is determined by what the audience must judge, which differs fundamentally between the two fields.

card.title: Design conventions across fields
back: The different presentation formats, drawing types and audiences appropriate to each design field.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 3: Design process: defining problems and developing ideas
points.title: The design brief
points.detail: The components of a brief: client, purpose, audience, context, constraints, deliverables and timeline.

questions.q: Name five components of a design brief and explain why constraints must be stated explicitly.
answer: A brief states the client, the communication purpose, the intended audience, the context of use and the required deliverables.
It also states constraints including budget, timeline, format, existing brand requirements and any legal obligations.
Explicit constraints prevent the designer from developing a concept that cannot be produced within the available resources.
They also provide the basis on which the final work is judged, since a solution that ignores a constraint has not met the brief.

card.title: The design brief
back: The components of a brief: client, purpose, audience, context, constraints, deliverables and timeline.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 3: Design process: defining problems and developing ideas
points.title: Understanding the audience
points.detail: Researching the demographics, needs, expectations and viewing context of the intended audience, and designing for them rather than for oneself.

questions.q: Explain how the viewing context of a design affects the decisions a designer makes.
answer: Viewing distance determines minimum type size and the level of detail that can be perceived.
Viewing duration determines how much information can be conveyed: a road sign has a second, a brochure has minutes.
The physical environment affects contrast and colour decisions, since a design viewed in bright sunlight or on a small phone screen has different requirements.
Designing without considering context typically produces work that succeeds on screen and fails in use.

card.title: Understanding the audience
back: Researching the demographics, needs, expectations and viewing context of the intended audience, and designing for them rather than for oneself.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 3: Design process: defining problems and developing ideas
points.title: Research methods
points.detail: Primary research through observation, interview and survey, and secondary research through precedent analysis and existing sources.

questions.q: Explain the value of analysing existing designs in the same field as part of research.
answer: It reveals the conventions of the field, which the audience already understands and expects.
It identifies what competitors are doing, so the new design can be differentiated rather than blending in.
It provides technical insight into production methods and formats that have proven effective in that context.

card.title: Research methods
back: Primary research through observation, interview and survey, and secondary research through precedent analysis and existing sources.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 3: Design process: defining problems and developing ideas
points.title: Visual research and inspiration
points.detail: Collecting and annotating visual references, building mood boards, and using them to establish direction without copying.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of a mood board and the distinction between inspiration and imitation.
answer: A mood board collects colours, typography, imagery and textures that establish the intended tone and visual direction of the project.
It communicates that direction to a client quickly and keeps the designer's decisions consistent through development.
Inspiration extracts a quality or principle and applies it to a new problem, while imitation reproduces another designer's solution, which is both unoriginal and potentially a breach of copyright.

card.title: Visual research and inspiration
back: Collecting and annotating visual references, building mood boards, and using them to establish direction without copying.

points.area: Unit 4: Delivering design solutions — AoS 1: Design process: refining and resolving design concepts
points.title: Giving and receiving critique
points.detail: Describing before judging, referring to the brief and criteria rather than personal taste, and using feedback to inform iteration.

questions.q: Explain how to give useful design critique and why 'I don't like it' is not critique.
answer: Begin by describing what the design does, identifying the choices made in composition, colour and typography.
Assess those choices against the brief and its stated criteria, including the intended audience and purpose.
Identify specifically what is working and what is not, and explain the reason in terms of the communication objective.
A statement of personal preference gives the designer nothing to act on, since it identifies neither the problem nor a direction for revision.

card.title: Giving and receiving critique
back: Describing before judging, referring to the brief and criteria rather than personal taste, and using feedback to inform iteration.

points.area: Unit 4: Delivering design solutions — AoS 1: Design process: refining and resolving design concepts
points.title: Evaluating against the brief
points.detail: Testing the resolved design against each requirement of the brief and each criterion, with evidence rather than assertion.

questions.q: Explain how to structure an evaluation of a finished design.
answer: Address each criterion from the brief separately rather than giving a general impression of the work.
State the evidence: what the design does, and whether the intended audience can be shown to respond as required.
Reach a clear judgement on each criterion, acknowledging where the solution falls short rather than defending every decision.
Identify what would be changed with more time or resources, which demonstrates critical understanding of the outcome.

card.title: Evaluating against the brief
back: Testing the resolved design against each requirement of the brief and each criterion, with evidence rather than assertion.

points.area: Unit 4: Delivering design solutions — AoS 2: Presenting design solutions
points.title: Presenting to a client
points.detail: Explaining the rationale behind design decisions, connecting them to the brief, and presenting work professionally and in context.

questions.q: Explain why a designer presents the rationale for decisions rather than just the finished work.
answer: The client judges the work against their business need, which they may not be able to assess from appearance alone.
Explaining how each decision serves the audience and purpose shifts the discussion from personal taste to whether the brief was met.
It also demonstrates that the solution resulted from research and reasoning rather than arbitrary preference, which builds confidence in the designer.

card.title: Presenting to a client
back: Explaining the rationale behind design decisions, connecting them to the brief, and presenting work professionally and in context.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 1: Professional design practice
points.title: Copyright and intellectual property
points.detail: Ownership of design work, the licensing of fonts and images, attribution, and the distinction between influence and infringement.

questions.q: Explain the copyright obligations that apply when a designer uses a font and a stock photograph in commercial work.
answer: Fonts are licensed rather than owned, and licences specify permitted uses such as desktop, web embedding or commercial distribution.
Using a font outside its licence terms, including one bundled with software, may breach the licence even though the file is installed.
Stock photographs require a licence appropriate to the use, since editorial licences typically exclude commercial and advertising use.
Model and property releases may also be required where identifiable people or private property appear in commercial work.

card.title: Copyright and intellectual property
back: Ownership of design work, the licensing of fonts and images, attribution, and the distinction between influence and infringement.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 1: Professional design practice
points.title: Ethical and cultural considerations
points.detail: Avoiding misleading communication and stereotyping, representing people respectfully, and the protocols surrounding cultural imagery.

questions.q: Explain two ethical obligations a designer has to the audience.
answer: Not to mislead: a design should not create a false impression through selective imagery, distorted data visualisation or deceptive layout.
To represent people respectfully, avoiding stereotype and considering how the depiction affects the group represented.
Cultural imagery, particularly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander designs and symbols, should not be appropriated, and use requires proper permission and consultation.
Accessibility is also an ethical obligation, since design that excludes people with impaired vision or colour perception denies them the information.

card.title: Ethical and cultural considerations
back: Avoiding misleading communication and stereotyping, representing people respectfully, and the protocols surrounding cultural imagery.

points.area: Unit 3: Visual communication in design practice — AoS 1: Professional design practice
points.title: Sustainability in design
points.detail: Material selection, production waste, the life of the product, design for disassembly and the environmental effect of design decisions.

questions.q: Explain three ways a designer can reduce the environmental impact of a printed publication.
answer: Specify recycled or certified stock and vegetable-based inks, reducing the impact of the materials used.
Design to standard sheet sizes so that trimming waste is minimised in production.
Reduce the number of colours and avoid laminates and foils that prevent the finished item from being recycled.
Consider whether the communication needs to be printed at all, or whether a digital format would meet the brief.

card.title: Sustainability in design
back: Material selection, production waste, the life of the product, design for disassembly and the environmental effect of design decisions.

points.area: Exam technique
points.title: Analysing an unseen design
points.detail: Describing what is present before interpreting it, using correct terminology for elements and principles, and linking each observation to purpose and audience.

questions.q: Explain the structure of a strong response analysing an unseen visual communication.
answer: Identify the design field, purpose and likely audience from the evidence in the image.
Describe specific choices using correct terminology, naming the elements and principles at work rather than describing impressionistically.
Explain the effect of each choice on the viewer and how it serves the communication purpose.

points.area: Exam technique
points.title: Using terminology precisely
points.detail: Naming elements and principles correctly, distinguishing them from one another, and avoiding vague descriptive language.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a design element and a design principle, and give two examples of each.
answer: Elements are the components from which a design is built, such as line, shape, form, colour, tone, texture and type.
Principles are the ways those components are arranged and related, such as balance, hierarchy, contrast, proximity, alignment and repetition.
A response that confuses the two, for example describing colour as a principle, indicates imprecise understanding.

questions.q: State three practical approaches to completing a drawing task under timed exam conditions.
answer: Construct lightly first, establishing proportion, horizon line and vanishing points before committing to any detail.
Work across the whole drawing at a consistent level of resolution rather than finishing one corner in detail and leaving the rest blank.
Reserve time to line in and clean up, since an accurate but unresolved drawing presents poorly and loses marks for finish.
